_doc: Closed misconception catalog (ADAPTIVE-tutoring G3). Every entry is anchored in the corpus: `corpus_quote` must appear verbatim in the `## Common Mistakes` section of corpus/<corpus_pattern>.md (enforced by tests/tutoring/test_catalog.py). Ids are stable: <pattern>.<slug>.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: Checking one key but reading another
misconceptions.name: Checking one key, reading another
misconceptions.correct_model: A membership test and the lookup that follows it must use the SAME key: once `complement in seen` is true, `seen[complement]` is the value you are allowed to read.
misconceptions.example: nums = [2, 7], target = 9. At i = 1, num = 7 and complement = 2. `2 in seen` is True, but `seen[7]` was never stored, so `seen[num]` raises KeyError while `seen[complement]` returns 0.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: Checking `if complement in nums` (O(n) list scan)
misconceptions.name: Scanning a list instead of a hash lookup
misconceptions.correct_model: `x in some_list` walks the whole list (O(n)); a dict or set answers the same question in O(1) on average, which is what makes the single pass O(n) overall.
misconceptions.example: For 10,000 numbers, `complement in nums[:i]` does up to 10,000 comparisons per step (about 50 million in total); `complement in seen` with a dict does one hash lookup per step.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: returning the two-sided `left + node + right` path to the parent
misconceptions.name: Returning the two-sided path to the parent
misconceptions.correct_model: The recursion has two jobs: RETURN the best one-sided path the parent can extend (`node + max(left, right, 0)`), and separately UPDATE a global best with the two-sided path through the node (`node + left + right`).
misconceptions.example: Tree 1 -> (2, 3). At node 1 the two-sided path 2 -> 1 -> 3 sums to 6, but if node 1 had a parent, that parent could only continue through ONE of 2 or 3 -- returning 6 would describe a path that forks, which is not a path.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: Forgetting the base case `if root is None: return ...`
misconceptions.name: Missing the empty-subtree base case
misconceptions.correct_model: Every recursive tree function must decide what an empty subtree (`None`) returns before touching `node.left` or `node.val`.
misconceptions.example: A leaf's children are None; calling `f(None)` without a base case evaluates `None.left` and raises AttributeError.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: skipping the parent NODE instead of the parent EDGE
misconceptions.name: Skipping the parent node instead of the parent edge
misconceptions.correct_model: In Tarjan's bridge-finding, the only edge to ignore is the one you arrived by. Identify it by its edge index, not by the parent's node id: a second (parallel) edge to the parent is a genuine back edge and must lower `low[u]`.
misconceptions.example: connections = [[0,1],[0,1]]: two separate cables between 0 and 1. Neither is critical. Skipping every edge back to node 0 ignores the second cable, keeps low[1] = 1 > disc[0] = 0, and wrongly reports [0,1] as a bridge.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: Marking a node visited when it's *dequeued* rather than *enqueued*
misconceptions.name: Marking visited on dequeue
misconceptions.correct_model: Mark a node visited at the moment you ENQUEUE it. Then each node enters the queue at most once, and the first time it is reached is already by the fewest edges.
misconceptions.example: A is connected to B and C, and both connect to D. Marking on dequeue: D is enqueued once from B and again from C before either copy is popped, so D (and everything after it) is processed twice.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: Reaching for DFS to find the fewest edges in an unweighted graph
misconceptions.name: Using DFS for an unweighted shortest path
misconceptions.correct_model: BFS visits nodes in order of distance (all nodes 1 edge away, then 2, ...), so the first time it reaches the target is along a fewest-edges path. DFS follows one branch as deep as it goes and can reach the target by a long route first.
misconceptions.example: Edges A-B, A-C, C-D, D-B. DFS from A that tries C first reaches B as A -> C -> D -> B (3 edges); BFS reaches B at distance 1.

misconceptions.corpus_quote: Marking a node visited *after* popping it instead of before pushing
misconceptions.name: Marking visited after the pop
misconceptions.correct_model: With an explicit stack, mark a node visited when you push it, so the same node cannot pile up on the stack from many neighbours. A check-and-skip after the pop avoids reprocessing but still lets the duplicates accumulate.
misconceptions.example: In a dense graph every unvisited neighbour pushes the same node again before it is popped, so the stack can hold O(E) copies instead of O(V) nodes.
